questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a new diagnosis of HIV and cerebral toxoplasmosis. He was started on sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine, as well as raltegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir. Three weeks later, he is admitted with nephrolithiasis.
questions.lead_in: Which of his medications would be most likely to cause development of renal stones?
questions.explanation: Sulfadiazine High-dose sulfonamides can cause crystalluria. Some antiretroviral agents can cause crystalluria as well, most notably indinavir and atazanavir. Aciclovir is another drug that can be associated with crystalluria.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q43

questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman presented with a widespread rash and facial swelling. She reported multiple lesions, which had started on her face, then spread throughout her body. She was on day 7 of trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole for treatment of recurrent axillary community-acquired MRSA furunculosis. She was known to have diabetes mellitus and was taking metformin. On examination, her temperature was 38.4°C, her blood pressure was 136/64 mmHg, and her heart rate was 72 beats/minute. She had facial edema and widespread erythematous maculopapular lesions. Investigations: Total white cell count 14.3 x109/L (70% eosinophils on differential) ALT 121 U/L Alkaline phosphatase 145 U/L
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
Skin lesions due to CA-MRSA sepsis and multiorgan dysfunction

questions.explanation: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) presents in a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations typically 1–8 weeks after the start of an offending medication. The triad of fever, rash, and internal organ involvement (renal, hematologic, and liver involvement most common) is suggestive. Current treatment recommendations include treatment with corticosteroids. Mortality can be as high as 10%, mostly due to liver failure. Many medications have been associated with DRESS including antibiotics (sulfonamides, minocycline, etc.), anticonvulsants, and other drugs. With no sepsis and stable vital signs both streptococcal toxic shock and sepsis with multiorgan dysfunction due to CA-MRSA infection are unlikely. Fixed drug eruption does not cause systemic repercussions and typically leads to more focalized lesions. The liver abnormalities and eosinophilia are part of the presentation for DRESS not TEN.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q27

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of dyspnea. His symptoms began as exertional dyspnea and dry cough but progressed to occurring at rest. He had ulcerative colitis and gout and was on treatment with infliximab. He had previously developed a Stevens–Johnson syndrome in response to sulfasalazine. He had also required blood transfusions after taking a new gout medication, which he could not remember. On examination, his respiratory rate was 32 breaths/ minute, and his oxygen saturation 85% on room air. Fine crepitations were heard throughout all lung fields. Investigations: Blood gas PaO2 55 mmHg (7.3kPa) Chest X-ray
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate therapy?
questions.explanation: Pentamidine This patient has severe pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP). PCP is associated with a variety of immunocompromising conditions. It is a potential complication of most immunosuppressants, including TNF-α-antagonists like infliximab. He has a history of severe allergy to sulfasalazine, a sulfa agent, and thus TMP–SMX should be avoided. His history also hints at possible G6PD deficiency (he developed hemolytic anemia after taking rasburicase). His clinical findings of hypoxia and bilateral reticular opacification suggest the diagnosis. His disease is classified as severe based on PaO2 <70 mmHg. Atovaquone is not indicated for use in severe PCP . It can only be used in mild PCP . Clindamycin and primaquine are appropriate alternatives to TMP–SMX in severe PCP , but G6PD deficiency should be ruled out before use of primaquine given the patient’s history which raises concern for this disorder. TMP + dapsone are not indicated in severe PCP . Additionally, G6PD deficiency should be ruled out before use of dapsone given the patient’s history. (Image from Kumar P , Clark M. Kumar & Clark’s Cases in Clinical Medicine. 3rd ed. Elsevier; 2013.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q26

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents with a 4-week history of worsening exertional dyspnea, dry cough, and mild fever. On examination his temperature is 37.9°C, his heart rate is 110 beats/minute, and his respiratory rate is 28 breaths/minute. Oxygen saturations are 90% on room air. He has oral candidiasis and small volume lymphadenopathy in his axillary, cervical, and inguinal chains. Auscultation of his chest is unremarkable. Investigations: Arterial blood gas PO2 (FiO2 room air) 7.8 kPa CXR: see radiograph below He is started empirically on intravenous trimethoprim– sulfamethoxazole (TMP–SMX) and methylprednisolone. On the second day of treatment he develops a widespread rash consistent with erythema multiforme, including oral ulceration and eye involvement. His TMP–SMX is identified as the likely cause.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment choice?

options.text: Continue TMP–SMX at a reduced dose of 90 mg/ kg per day
Start immediate desensitization regimen for TMP–SMX

questions.explanation: Switch to clindamycin plus primaquine This is the correct answer as the patient has presented with features of severe PCP and has developed a severe (grade 4) reaction to first-line treatment with TMP–SMX. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q35

questions.question: A young man presents with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and a new diagnosis of HIV. He is hypoxemic, requiring 4 L of O2 to maintain saturations >90%.
questions.question_raw: Young guy presents with PJP and new diagnosis of HIV. He is hypoxemic requiring 4L of O2 to remain >90% sats.

parts.text: He had a full-body rash without mucous membrane involvement previously on a sulfa drug. Name 4 treatment regimens or strategies you can use.
When is the ideal time to start ART?
He is now fully recovered. Name 2 criteria for when you can stop PCP prophylaxis.

parts_raw.text: He had a full body rash without mucous membrane involvement previously on a sulfa drug. Name 4 treatment regimens or strategies you can use (2)
When is the ideal time to start ART (1)
He is now fully recovered. Name 2 criteria when you can stop PCP prophylaxis (1)

questions.model_answer: a) His disease is moderate-to-severe (PaO2 ≤70 mm Hg / requiring 4 L O2), and his prior reaction was non-life-threatening (no mucous membrane involvement), so: (1) TMP-SMX desensitization then full-dose TMP-SMX; (2) IV clindamycin plus primaquine (preferred alternative for moderate-to-severe PCP; check G6PD); (3) IV pentamidine 4 mg/kg daily; (4) TMP plus dapsone (with caution given sulfonamide intolerance; check G6PD). All warrant adjunctive corticosteroids. b) Start ART early — within 2 weeks of initiating PCP treatment (once clinically stable), balancing benefit against IRIS risk. c) Any one of: (1) CD4 count risen from <200 to >200 cells/mm3 and maintained for >3 months on ART; (2) CD4 count 100-200 cells/mm3 with HIV plasma RNA below the limit of detection (<50 copies/mL) for 3-6 months.
questions.beyond_mandell: Ideal ART timing (within ~2 weeks of PCP therapy) rests on IDSA/NIH/CDC Opportunistic Infection guidelines; the chapter notes IRIS risk with early ART but does not state the interval.

cohort_answer.text: Treatment options (severe infection if requiring 4L O2): Desensitize to septra; Primaquine + IV clindamycin; IV pentamidine; Dapsone + Trimethoprim (Atovaquone not a great answer in this setting, too unwell). Ideal ART start: When stable and within 2 weeks of starting treatment for PJP. Stop prophylaxis criteria: CD4 counts increased from <200 cells/mm3 to >200 cells/mm3 for >3 months as a result of ART

questions.question: A drug shortage occurs in your hospital.

parts.text: How would you treat PJP (Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia), Toxoplasma, and Stenotrophomonas if TMP-SMX (Septra), sulfadiazine, and ticarcillin-clavulanic acid/TMP-SMX respectively were not available? Give two options for each.

parts_raw.text: How would you treat PJP, Toxoplasma, and Stenotrophomonas if Septra, Sulfadiazine, and Ticarcillin-clavulanic acid/Septra respectively were not available (2 options each)?

questions.model_answer: a) PJP without TMP-SMX (TMP-SMX is normally first-line): (1) IV pentamidine; (2) clindamycin plus primaquine [atovaquone or trimethoprim-dapsone are further alternatives, typically for mild-to-moderate disease]. b) Toxoplasmosis without sulfadiazine (standard induction is pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin): (1) pyrimethamine + clindamycin + leucovorin (preferred sulfa-sparing regimen); (2) high-dose TMP-SMX (an effective alternative for AIDS-related cerebral toxoplasmosis). c) Stenotrophomonas maltophilia without TMP-SMX or ticarcillin-clavulanate (TMP-SMX is the recommended agent, and TMP-SMX + ticarcillin-clavulanate has been used in cancer patients): (1) levofloxacin (fluoroquinolone); (2) minocycline or tigecycline.
questions.beyond_mandell: The chapter names only TMP-SMX and ticarcillin-clavulanate for S. maltophilia; levofloxacin, minocycline/tigecycline (and cefideromycin) as alternatives rest on IDSA AMR guidance, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: PJP (cannot use Septra): Pentamidine; Atovaquone. Toxoplasma (cannot use Sulfadiazine): Pyrimethamine + clindamycin + leucovorin; Atovaquone + septra + leucovorin; Atovaquone +/- pyrimethamine + Septra + leucovorin. Stenotrophomonas (cannot use Ticarcillin-clavulanic acid or Septra): Tigecycline (black box for death); Levofloxacin; Minocycline
